title: Machine-learning estimates connect campaign spending effects to possible shifts in congressional control
summary: The authors used flexible machine-learning estimates of heterogeneous campaign-spending effects and aggregated them across U.S. House and Senate elections. They report nonlinear marginal effects at the campaign level and counterfactual seat swings that could have changed party control at historically observed spending levels; such conditions appear less common in the last decade. These are model-based observational counterfactuals and do not prove that spending causally determines election outcomes.
ai_technology: Flexible machine-learning estimation of heterogeneous campaign-spending effects

evidence.tested: The primary paper reports robustness analyses across alternative machine-learning methods and counterfactual aggregation of estimated campaign-level spending effects to congressional seat totals.
evidence.unknown: The analyses are observational counterfactual estimates and do not establish that campaign spending causally determines election outcomes.
evidence.ai_role: Flexible machine-learning models estimate heterogeneous, nonlinear campaign-spending effects that are aggregated to the congressional level.
